# How to write a wedding speech or toast that sounds like you

> **In short:** You can draft a heartfelt wedding speech in about 30 minutes by sharing a handful of specific memories with any AI assistant and editing the draft until it sounds like your own voice. The AI drafts; the voice is yours.

You're standing at a table with a glass in your hand and a phone full of photos, and suddenly the room is looking at you. The good news is that writing a wedding speech has gotten a lot easier with an AI assistant, and you don't need to be a writer to sound warm and natural. Here's a calm, step-by-step approach that takes about half an hour from blank page to ready-to-deliver.

## Before you start
- **Any free AI assistant on your phone or laptop** — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or one you already use. No special plan needed for this.
- **About 30 minutes total** — roughly 10 to gather stories, 15 working with the AI, and 5 to edit and rehearse.
- **A short list of 3–5 memories** about the couple. A quick note on your phone is fine — don't overthink it.
- **Knowing who else is speaking** (optional but helpful), so your stories don't repeat theirs.

## Step 1 — Gather your favorite memories
Grab your phone or a notebook and jot down 3–5 short memories about the couple. They don't need to be deep — small, specific moments work best: the time your friend burned the Thanksgiving turkey, the look on their face when they got the job, the inside joke about the broken umbrella. Don't filter yourself yet; just write whatever pops up. After a few minutes, pick the three that make you smile the most, or that show who they really are.

💬 Example: "1. Sam burned the Thanksgiving turkey in 2019. 2. Pat laughed so hard at our movie night that milk came out of their nose. 3. The first time I met Pat, Sam couldn't stop talking about them for an hour."

If it looks different: if you're writing on paper, plain bullet points are perfect. If you have photos of the couple, scroll through them — they usually jog the best memories faster than you expect.

You'll know it worked when you have a short list you actually like, not a list of "should" memories you think you're supposed to tell.

## Step 2 — Open a fresh chat with your AI assistant
Open any AI assistant you have access to — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or whichever one you already use — and start a brand-new conversation. Don't reuse an old chat about something else, because earlier context can confuse the assistant. You should see a clean text box, usually with a placeholder like "Ask anything" or "Message [assistant]". Tap or click into that box to start.

💬 Example: "I need help drafting a wedding speech. Start a new chat for me."

If it looks different: on a phone the box is usually at the bottom of the screen; on a laptop it's the big central box. If you're already inside an older conversation, look for a "+ New chat" or "New conversation" button — usually near the top-left or in a sidebar.

You'll know it worked when you see a blinking cursor in an empty message box, with no previous messages above it.

## Step 3 — Share the context in one clear prompt
Now type one prompt that gives the assistant everything it needs: your relationship to the couple, where the wedding is (just briefly), how long the speech should be, the tone you want, and the memories you collected. Hit send. You'll see the assistant start typing back within a few seconds. The more specific your prompt, the less editing you'll need later — vague prompts lead to vague speeches.

💬 Example: "I'm the best man at Sam and Pat's wedding next Saturday, a small outdoor reception with about 60 guests. I want a warm, slightly funny 5-minute toast (around 650 words). Tone: like I'm talking to friends, not reading an essay. Here are 3 memories to weave in: [1] Sam burned the Thanksgiving turkey in 2019, [2] Pat laughed so hard at our movie night that milk came out of their nose, [3] when I first met Pat, Sam wouldn't stop talking about them for an hour."

If it looks different: if the assistant splits your message into awkward chunks, that's normal — just keep typing or send the next part as a follow-up. Some assistants let you paste long prompts in one go; others ask you to "continue" after a soft character limit.

You'll know it worked when the assistant asks any clarifying questions (like whether anyone else is giving a speech) or starts drafting right away.

## Step 4 — Ask for a first draft with the tone you want
If the assistant asked questions, answer them first. Then ask for the full draft in one piece, and add a small instruction about tone if your first prompt didn't include one — "please don't use big words", "keep sentences short", "more stories, fewer general statements", or "make me sound like a real person, not a textbook". After a few seconds you'll see a complete speech appear, usually around 600–800 words.

💬 Example: "Now write the full speech. Keep it warm and grounded. Use my exact memories. Don't make me sound like a news anchor."

If it looks different: if the speech comes back too long, reply "cut it to 5 minutes, about 650 words" and send again. If it sounds too formal, ask for "more casual — like I'm talking to friends at a backyard barbecue." The assistant can adjust in seconds.

You'll know it worked when there's a complete speech in front of you — even if parts of it sound a bit off, that's normal and easy to fix in the next step.

## Step 5 — Read it aloud and make it sound like you
This is the step that turns an AI draft into your speech. Read the draft out loud, slowly, in the room where you actually are. Anywhere a sentence feels too stiff, too formal, or too "writerly", change it to something you'd actually say at a dinner table. Cut any jokes that feel forced. Add the small words you naturally use — "honestly", "look", "you know", "the thing is". Most speeches need about 10–20 small edits to feel real.

💬 Example: change "It is a privilege to stand before you all this evening" to "I'm not going to lie, I'm a bit nervous, so bear with me."

If it looks different: if you don't know what to fix, read it to a friend and ask "where does it stop sounding like me?" Their answer usually pinpoints 2–3 sentences that need work. If nothing feels wrong, it's probably already good.

You'll know it worked when you can read the whole thing out loud without stumbling over a single sentence.

## Step 6 — Practice once and bring simple notes
Read the final version out loud one more time, all the way through, while timing yourself with a phone timer or stopwatch. A 5-minute speech usually runs 600–700 words; if you're well over or under, ask the AI to trim or expand and repeat. On the day, don't read from your phone screen word-for-word — print or write a simple outline with just the opening line, the memories in order, and the closing line. Looking up to make eye contact matters more than memorizing every word.

💬 Example: outline = "Open: thank you, how I know them. Story 1: Thanksgiving turkey. Story 2: movie night. Story 3: how they met Pat. Close: toast."

If it looks different: if you'd rather memorize the whole thing, that's fine too — but most people speak more naturally with notes in hand. If you tend to ramble, write down a one-word reminder for each section ("turkey — movie — Pat — toast") so you stay on track.

You'll know it worked when you've read the speech once without losing your place, and your outline fits on a small card.

## Common mistakes
- **Writing like a school essay instead of a speech.** Read every sentence out loud as you edit — if you wouldn't say it at a dinner table, change it.
- **Forgetting to time yourself.** A 5-minute speech is roughly 600–700 words. Read it once with a stopwatch before the wedding day, not during it.
- **Including inside jokes only half the room will get.** If a joke needs three minutes of backstory, cut it or explain it in one short sentence — otherwise half the guests tune out.
- **Forgetting to say the couple's names out loud.** Names sound beautiful in a speech. If your draft never says "Sam" or "Pat", sprinkle them in naturally.
- **Trying too hard to be funny.** Forced humor lands worse than sincere warmth. If a joke doesn't come naturally, leave it out — a real story always beats a strained punchline.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the same approach works for any short personal speech — retirement parties, baby showers, 50th birthdays, even a quick eulogy. The skill is "collect memories, draft with help, edit until it sounds like you", and it transfers everywhere.
- **For your business or work:** you can use the same prompt structure to draft a short opening for a team meeting, a thank-you speech at a retirement lunch, or a few warm words for a colleague leaving the company.
- **If you're just getting started:** pick the three memories that always make you smile when you tell them — those are your best material, and they'll carry the speech even if every other line is rough.

## Try it now
Open your AI assistant right now and type: "Help me write a 5-minute wedding speech for [name], who is my [relationship]. The couple met [in a coffee shop / at work / through friends], and here are 3 memories: [memory 1], [memory 2], [memory 3]." Then read the draft out loud once and change any sentence you wouldn't actually say. That's the whole skill — and you've already started.
